chapters.name: Chapter 1: Know the risks and check the work

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The main risks of AI in a business
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the main AI risks and find where they show up in your business.
This lesson builds toward: Given at least three ways your business uses AI, you will list the main AI risks that apply and rate how serious each one is, with one check written for every serious risk.
Five risks show up again and again. Accuracy: AI can make up facts, prices or rules. Fairness: AI can treat groups of people unfairly because of patterns in what it learned. Privacy: customer data you type in may be stored or used. Honesty: marketing claims about AI, or AI-made reviews, can mislead. Ownership: who owns AI-made work, and whether it copies someone else's.
Being ethical with AI means being honest, fair and careful with people's information, and keeping a human responsible. Usually, doing the ethical thing also keeps you on the right side of the law.
Make a risk list for your business: where you use AI, what could go wrong, how bad it would be, and what check you will add.
Step by step:
- List every place you use or plan to use AI.
- For each, ask which of the five risks apply.
- Rate how bad a mistake would be: low, medium or high.
- Write one check for each medium or high risk.
Words to know:
- Ethics: ideas about what is right and fair.
- Risk: something that could go wrong, and how much harm it would cause.
- Bias: results that are unfair to some groups of people.
Try it now: Make a risk list with at least three ways your business uses AI. Mark which of the five risks apply, rate each, and write one check for the serious ones.
You can now name the main AI risks and map them to your own business.

check.q: Which is a privacy risk of AI in a business?
options: Customer details leaking through an AI tool
check.why: Putting customer data into AI tools can expose it.

check.q: Your AI chatbot answers customers' delivery questions. How do you treat this on your risk list?
options: Leave it off; it is just a chatbot
List it, rate it and write a check for wrong answers
check.why: Anything customers see goes on the risk list with a check.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Checking AI work for accuracy and fairness
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up a human review step that catches wrong facts and unfair results.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI output that customers see or that affects a decision, you will check it for wrong facts, wrong math, unprovable claims and unfair results, using a written review step and keeping hiring, lending and housing decisions with a person.
Anything AI makes that a customer will see, or that affects money, law, health or safety, needs a human check. Check facts against your own records or official sources, redo the math, and remove any claim you cannot prove.
Check for fairness too. If you use AI to screen job applicants, set prices, approve customers or write job ads, look at whether it treats people differently because of race, sex, age, disability, religion, national origin or similar traits. Anti-discrimination laws still apply when a computer helps make the decision.
For high-stakes decisions, such as hiring, firing, lending, housing or anything about health, do not let AI decide. Use it to organize information, keep the decision with a person, and talk to a lawyer about the rules that apply to you.
Step by step:
- Mark which AI outputs customers see or that affect money, law, health or safety.
- For those, check facts, math and claims every time.
- Look at AI-assisted decisions for unfair differences between groups.
- Keep high-stakes decisions with a person.
- Ask a lawyer about rules for hiring, lending or housing decisions.
Words to know:
- Human review: a person checks AI work before it is used.
- High-stakes decision: a choice that seriously affects someone's job, money, home or health.
- Discrimination: treating people unfairly because of who they are.
Try it now: Pick one AI output your customers see. Check it for facts, math, unprovable claims and unfair wording. Write the review step you will use every time.
You can now review AI work for accuracy and fairness before it affects customers or decisions.

check.q: What is bias in an AI result?
options: A result that is unfair to some groups
check.why: Bias means AI treats some groups of people unfairly.

check.q: AI ranks job applicants for you. What do you do?
options: Check the ranking for unfairness and make the decision yourself
check.why: A person makes hiring decisions, and anti-discrimination laws still apply.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Protecting customer data
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Decide what data may and may not go into AI tools, using the FTC's five principles.
This lesson builds toward: Given the customer information you hold, you will write a never-in-AI list and check the privacy settings of your main AI tool, following the FTC's five data principles.
The FTC's guide for businesses on protecting personal information has five principles: take stock (know what personal information you have), scale down (keep only what you need), lock it (protect what you keep), pitch it (dispose of what you no longer need) and plan ahead (have a plan for a security problem).
Apply them to AI. Do not put Social Security numbers, card or bank numbers, passwords, health details or full customer contact lists into AI chat tools. Use placeholders or summaries. Check each tool's privacy settings and terms, and prefer business plans that promise not to train on your data if you must use customer information.
Be honest in your own privacy notice: if you use AI tools that process customer information, say so. Privacy laws differ by state and country; ask a lawyer what applies to you.
Step by step:
- Take stock: list the customer information you hold.
- Scale down: stop collecting what you do not need.
- Write a never-in-AI list: ID numbers, card and bank numbers, passwords, health details.
- Check each AI tool's privacy settings and terms.
- Make a short plan for what you will do if data leaks.
Words to know:
- Personal information: details that identify a person, like name with address, ID numbers or card numbers.
- Privacy notice: a statement telling customers what data you collect and how you use it.
- Security incident: when data is lost, stolen or seen by someone who should not see it.
Official sources:
- FTC: Protecting Personal Information, A Guide for Business
Try it now: Take stock of the customer information you hold, write your never-in-AI list, and check the privacy settings of the AI tool you use most.
You can now decide what customer data may go into AI tools and protect the rest.

check.q: What does "scale down" mean in the FTC's data principles?
options: Keep only the information you need
check.why: Keeping less data means less can be lost.

check.q: You want AI to summarize customer emails. What do you check first?
options: The tool's privacy terms and settings for training on your data
check.why: Know how a tool stores and uses data before customer information goes in.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Honest claims, ownership and your policy

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Honest AI claims, endorsements and reviews
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check your marketing for misleading AI claims, undisclosed endorsements and fake reviews.
This lesson builds toward: Given your website or social posts, you will mark every AI or results claim keep, fix or remove, and check paid posts and reviews, so every claim is true and provable, every paid post is clearly disclosed and no review is fake or bought.
The FTC says advertising must be truthful, not misleading, and backed by evidence, and that applies to AI claims. Do not say your product "uses AI" if it does not, and do not exaggerate what AI does or how accurate it is. In 2026 the FTC finalized orders against firms that claimed their AI marketing service listened to people's conversations through smart devices, when it did not.
If you pay or give free products to someone to promote you, the connection must be clearly disclosed, such as "#ad" at the start of a post or in the video itself. You are responsible for what your promoters say.
The FTC's rule on fake reviews bans fake reviews and testimonials, including AI-generated reviews from people who do not exist, and bans rewards given only for positive reviews. Talk to a lawyer if you are unsure whether a claim or campaign is allowed.
Step by step:
- List every claim your marketing makes about AI or results.
- Keep only claims that are true and that you can prove.
- Check that every paid or gifted promotion has a clear disclosure.
- Make sure every review is real and was not paid for with a reward for a good rating.
- Ask a lawyer when unsure.
Words to know:
- Substantiate: back up a claim with evidence.
- Material connection: a link like payment or free products between a business and someone who promotes it.
Official sources:
- FTC: Advertising and Marketing Basics
- FTC: Orders against Cox Media Group and two other firms over AI marketing claims (2026)
- FTC: Endorsement Guides, What People Are Asking
- FTC: Final rule banning fake reviews and testimonials (press release)
Try it now: Go through your website or social posts. List each claim about AI or results, and mark it keep (true and provable), fix, or remove. Check any paid post for a clear disclosure.
You can now check your marketing for honest AI claims, proper disclosures and real reviews.

check.q: What makes an AI claim in an ad acceptable under FTC rules?
options: It is true, not misleading and backed by evidence
check.why: FTC advertising rules apply to AI claims like any other.

check.q: A creator you paid posts about your shop without a disclosure. What do you do?
options: Ask them to add a clear disclosure such as "#ad" at the start
check.why: The business is responsible for what its paid promoters say.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Copyright and AI-made work
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain who can own AI-assisted work and how to reduce copying risks.
This lesson builds toward: Given business assets made with AI, you will explain who can own AI-assisted work and plan the human creative work you will add, noting any asset that needs a lawyer's advice.
The US Copyright Office's report on copyrightability (January 2025) says copyright protects human authorship. Purely AI-generated material is not protected, and simply writing a prompt does not make you the author of the output. But using AI as a tool does not block protection: your own creative arrangement, edits, or human-made work that shows in the result can be protected.
What this means for a business: if you need to own something, such as your logo, product designs or a book, put real human creativity into it and keep records of what you did. When registering a work that includes AI-generated material, the Office has guidance about disclosing it.
The other risk is copying. AI output can sometimes look like someone else's work or brand. Do not ask AI to copy a living artist, a brand's logo or a famous character, and check important outputs. Copyright law around AI is still changing, with court cases ongoing; talk to a lawyer before relying on AI-made work for something important.
Step by step:
- Mark which business assets you need to own (logo, designs, books, courses).
- For those, add real human creative work and keep notes or drafts.
- Do not ask AI to copy a specific artist, brand or character.
- Check important outputs for resemblance to others' work.
- Talk to a lawyer before registering or relying on AI-assisted work.
Words to know:
- Copyright: the legal right to control copying of an original creative work.
- Human authorship: creative choices made by a person, which copyright protects.
- Register: file a work with the Copyright Office to record your claim.
Official sources:
- US Copyright Office: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence
- US Copyright Office: Part 2 Copyrightability report announcement (January 2025)
Try it now: List three business assets you have made or plan to make with AI. For each, write whether you need to own it and what human creative work you will add, and note any that need a lawyer's advice.
You can now explain the basics of copyright for AI-made work and lower your copying risk.

check.q: According to the US Copyright Office, what is protected in AI-assisted work?
check.why: Human creative work can be protected; purely AI-generated material is not.

check.q: You need to own your new logo. What do you do?
options: Use a pure AI image as it is
Add real human creative work, keep records and ask a lawyer if unsure
check.why: Human creative work and records make protection more likely; a lawyer can advise.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Writing your AI use policy
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page AI use policy for your business.
This lesson builds toward: For your own business, you will write a one-page AI use policy with all seven parts, naming who is responsible, when to ask a lawyer and a review date.
An AI use policy is a short set of rules for how you and anyone who works with you use AI. It turns everything in this course into habits. It helps new helpers, reassures customers, and shows you took care if something goes wrong.
A simple policy has seven parts: approved tools; never-in-AI information; outputs that always need a human check; honest claims and disclosures; copyright and ownership; who to ask when unsure (including a lawyer); and a review date.
AI can draft it: give it your risk list and the rules from this course and ask for a one-page policy in plain words. Then edit it so every rule is something you will really do, share it with anyone who helps you, and review it every six months.
Step by step:
- Gather your risk list, never-in-AI list and claims check from earlier lessons.
- Ask AI for a one-page policy with the seven parts, in plain words.
- Edit every rule so it is true for your business.
- Share it with anyone who helps you.
- Set a review date six months from now.
Words to know:
- AI use policy: a short set of rules for how a business uses AI.
- Review date: the day you will check and update the policy.
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page AI use policy with all seven parts, edit it to fit your business, and set a review date.
You can now run your business's AI use under a clear, honest, written policy, and know when to call a lawyer.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Approved tools and data No list of approved tools or no never-in-AI list. Approved tools named and a clear list of information that must never go into them. Notes the privacy setting checked in each approved tool. Human checks Does not say which outputs need a person to check them. Facts, money, legal, health and anything customers see all need a human check. Names who checks and what they look for, including fairness. Honest claims and endorsements No rule on AI claims, paid endorsements or reviews. Claims must be true and provable; paid posts disclosed; no fake or bought reviews. Includes the results of the owner's keep, fix or remove review. Copyright No rule for AI-made content. Says when human creative work is added and when to ask a lawyer about ownership. Lists the business's key AI-assisted assets and how each is handled. Responsibility and review No one named as responsible, or no review date. Names who is responsible, when to call a lawyer and a review date. Links back to the risk list so each serious risk has a rule. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is an AI use policy?
options: A list of AI tool prices
A written set of rules for how your business uses AI
check.why: A policy tells everyone how AI is used safely in the business.

check.q: A new AI tool comes out that your staff want to use. What does your policy tell you to do?
options: Let everyone try it with customer data
Check it against the policy before adding it to the approved list
check.why: The policy lists approved tools and how new ones are added.
